newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir steadied, lights back on as crew fix blunder.
newsitem.headline: Mir steadied, lights back on as crew fix blunder.

text.p: The accident-prone crew of Russia's Mir space station finally arrested their tumble through space on Friday, locking the crippled ship's solar panels on to the Sun and switching the lights back on.
"We solved the problem," NASA official Mark Severance told Reuters at Russian Mission Control outside Moscow.
"Things are going real well. I'm really pleased."

Flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin, 39, toiled through the night to reconnect most of Mir's life-support systems some 24 hours after one of the three crew -- it is not clear who -- mistakenly pulled out a cable and crashed the on-board computer.

Russian commander Vasily Tsibliyev, who was diagnosed with a probably stress-induced heart condition this week, and NASA physicist Michael Foale went to bed around midnight Moscow time (2000 GMT) while Lazutkin carried on working for another four and a half hours before breaking for a much-needed rest.
The mission doctor said the crew would take the weekend off.

Thursday's pulled plug threw the sprawling and already underpowered 140-tonne complex into a spin, depriving its solar panels of a steady stream of rays. It forced the crew to switch off systems and rely on back-up from their Soyuz escape capsule.

After slowly recharging its batteries, the station, which has suffered a jinx-like sequence of mishaps culminating in a near-fatal collision on June 25, is now being held in alignment to the Sun by electronically controlled motors.

A senior Russian Mission Control official, who declined to be identified, said the gyroscopic system that orients Mir without using precious fuel at all, would be reconnected late on Friday and other systems would come on after that.
"They have fully set up the orientation," the official said. "The electrical systems are gathering energy from the Sun."
By the end of the day Mir should be back in the situation it was in on Wednesday, when Tsibliyev was pulled from a two-man team to repair some of the collision damage due to his illness.
Foale was asked to step in for the risky job of mending severed power cables alongside Lazutkin.
Thursday's calamity may have delayed plans for completing the job next week, but this is not yet clear.
Lazutkin, on his first space mission, literally had a baptism of fire when a serious blaze broke out during his first days on Mir in February.

The moustachioed rocket scientist and former competitive gymnast has been denied the western media focus on Foale and the attention given to commander Tsibliyev, who runs most of the crew's communications with Mission Control, including frequent sharp exchanges with Earth.

But it is Lazutkin who could face the most dangerous task now in opening up the Spektr scientific module, sealed off on June 25 when a remote-controlled cargo craft being manoeuvred by Tsibliyev slammed into it and punctured its hermetic seal.
The cosmonauts do not know what conditions are like in Spektr, what poisonous substances or sharp objects may be floating about in its cramped airless interior.

Lazutkin, backed up by Foale, both wearing clumsy spacesuits, was due sometime around July 24 to go into Spektr and try to rconnect cables to three solar panels, whose loss has cut Mir's power supply by up to half at present.

Space officials met on Friday morning to discuss the preparations for the repairs, for which Foale needs intensive special training, and will meet again on Monday. They have said it is possible the job could be put off for a Russian-French crew due to arrive on August 7.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted a Mission Control official saying the Frenchman could even be dropped, allowing his two Russian colleagues to fly in more equipment.
"Changes in the flight plan are always possible," Vladimir Solovyov, the mission director, told a news conference.
The series of mishaps has raised questions over whether Mir should be ditched before a new international space station is launched next year.
Russian officials, whose agency depends on the foreign cash Mir brings in to keep much of the post-Soviet space industry aloft, insist they do not want to abandon the station.
